items.title: Arturo O'Farrill interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2024
items.q: as eloquent as any Beethoven piano sonata

ctx.x: Without a doubt much of the information that we have in the thing we call jazz comes from European melodicism. It comes from the chromatic, you know chromatic harmony. So in some ways this is funny that you said that because I was just listening to “Isfahan”

and I was just again — I was listening to “Isfahan” and “Warm Valley” and I was thinking about one of the greatest gifts of music is Duke Ellington’s sense of melodicism. Just the pacing and the outlaying of a Duke Ellington melody, to me, is as elegant as anything that Beethoven wrote and I’m a classically trained musician. My degrees are in classical music. But when I listen to Duke Ellington I can’t help but think this is classical music. It’s — you don’t have to dress it up. It’s already arrived fully formed…

That’s pretty profound. Thank you for that. I’m envious on a couple levels but one is that you’ve written for the dance. And I wonder if in your career before those commissions, if you ever were a dance — a pianist for a dance company, just accompanying their workouts and providing music for them to move to?
